newsitem.title: PERU: Peru declares regions in emergency for "El Nino".
newsitem.headline: Peru declares regions in emergency for "El Nino".

text.p: The Peruvian government declared nine of its 24 regions in emergency Friday to speed the nation's preparations for the harmful "El Nino" weather system that is expected to form later this year.

A decree in the official daily El Peruano said the measure applied to the northern regions of Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad and Ancash, and the southern regions of Arequipa, Moquegua, Tacna and Puno.

The state of emergency was needed "to prevent the effects of the possible climatic changes that the imminent presence of the Nino phenomenon will cause," the decree said. "It is necessary to adopt the necessary measures and actions to counteract the foreseeable natural disasters."
The measure will allow local authorities to begin immediately all practical preparations for El Nino.

The weather phenomenon causes droughts in the south of Peru and heavy rainfalls in the country's north. It can also affect crops and homes in the southern United Sates, northeastern Brazil, southeastern Africa and the west Pacific.

Friday's decree followed President Alberto Fujimori's formation earlier this week of a special commission -- joining the presidency, agriculture, transport and defense ministries -- to prepare for El Nino.
Fujimori warned Thursday that Peru's short-term economic growth prospects would depend on the effects of El Nino.

There are strong signs the weather system -- which ocurrs every two to seven years and is caused by a warming of waters in the Pacific -- is starting. But its strength will not be known until August, according to local meteorologists.
The phenomenon has been called El Nino, the Spanish name for the Christ child, because it usually occurs late in the year near Christmas.
The system's strength can vary dramatically. In 1986-87, El Nino formed but was barely noticed in Peru, while in 1982-83 its widespread damage caused the economy to contract more than 12 percent.
If Peru experiences an El Nino this year, the effects would last about 18 months and likely be strongest from December to March, experts say.
On shore, cotton, sugar, potato and fruit crops would likely suffer most. At sea, the climatic changes could drive fish away from Peru's waters, ruining small businesses in the industry.
Fishing is Peru's second largest production sector after mining.

The new government commission has an initial budget of $19 million and will focus its preventive work on improving agricultural infrastructure by repairing irrigation channels, strengthening bridges, and other projects.
